blocks.title: Volumetric analysis, indicator and end point
blocks.text: Volumetric analysis finds the concentrations of solutions by titration: a solution of unknown concentration is combined slowly and carefully with a known volume of a standard solution until a colour change shows the completion of the reaction. The substance that indicates the completion of the reaction by its change of colour is the indicator, and the moment at which the indicator changes colour is the end point. Either solution can be taken in the burette, with the other in a conical or titration flask.

Phenolphthalein solution is prepared by adding one gram of the indicator to 500 cm3 of 50% ethanol; only one to two drops are used in 10 cm3 of the solution to be titrated. Its colour changes from pink to colourless as the pH decreases. The light pink colour that marks the end point tends to fade gradually because atmospheric carbon dioxide slowly dissolves in the solution.
Materials: burette, pipette, funnel, conical flask, HCl solution, NaOH solution, phenolphthalein.

items: Rinse the pipette first with distilled water and then with the given NaOH solution.
Rinse the conical flask with distilled water only.
Pipette 10 cm3 of the NaOH solution into the conical flask.
Add one to two drops of phenolphthalein; the solution turns pink.
Rinse the burette first with distilled water and then with the given HCl solution.
Fix the burette upright on a clamp stand.
Fill it with the HCl solution through a funnel, then remove the funnel.
Using the tap at the base, let some acid flow into a beaker to remove any air bubble in the nozzle.
Note the burette reading as the initial reading, using an anti-parallax card or a white paper.
Place the conical flask on a white paper under the burette to see the colour change clearly; check that the burette does not leak.
Carry out a rough titration by adding the acid from the burette dropwise to the flask.
Swirl the contents of the flask while adding acid for thorough mixing.

Keep adding acid until the colour of the solution becomes light pink persistently: the end point. Note the burette reading as the final reading; final minus initial reading is the volume of acid used.

blocks.text: Repeat the titration to get accurate and concordant readings: at least three concordant readings that agree with one another within 0.1 cm3. The observations are tabulated as rough, 1, 2, 3 with final reading x, initial reading y and volume of acid used (x - y), giving the volume of HCl solution used in cm3.

blocks.alt: Left: a burette of HCl on a clamp stand above a conical flask of pink NaOH on white paper, with labels for rinsing, reading the meniscus and the tap. Top middle: indicator, end point and phenolphthalein. Top right: the readings table with rough, 1, 2 and 3 and the concordant-reading rule. Bottom: the equation, the molarity relation with its symbols, and the materials and rinsing rule.
blocks.caption: Acid-base titration of NaOH with HCl using phenolphthalein (original diagram after topic 16.5 and Figure 16.6).
blocks.long_description: Ten cubic centimetres of sodium hydroxide are pipetted into a conical flask with a drop or two of phenolphthalein, which turns it pink, and hydrochloric acid is run in from a burette, drop by drop near the end, while the flask is swirled over white paper. The end point is the last persistent light pink; the volume used is the final reading minus the initial, read at eye level with an anti-parallax card. A rough titration is followed by repeats until three readings agree within one-tenth of a cubic centimetre. Since the equation shows one mole of acid per mole of base, the molarity of the base follows from the molarity and volume of the acid and the volume of base by the relation between the two molarity-volume products divided by their mole numbers.

blocks.title: Molarity equation
blocks.text: M1 V1 / n1 = M2 V2 / n2, where M1, V1 and n1 are the molarity, the volume used and the number of moles in the balanced equation for the acid, and M2, V2 and n2 the same for the base. The molarity of the given base solution is M2 = M1 V1 n2 / (n1 V2).

blocks.caption: Rinsing and reading rules
rows: rinse with distilled water, then with the NaOH it will hold
rinse with distilled water, then with the HCl it will hold; remove the funnel; run out the air bubble
anti-parallax card or white paper; initial and final; at least three concordant readings within 0.1 cm3

blocks.prompt: Define indicator and end point, say what a concordant reading is, and explain why the flask is rinsed with water only (Quick Check 16.2a, b; MCQ I, II; exercise Q.2d).
blocks.explanation: An indicator is a substance whose colour change shows that the reaction is complete; the end point is the moment the indicator changes colour. Concordant readings are repeated titration volumes that agree with one another within 0.1 cm3. The flask is rinsed only with water because any NaOH left from rinsing would add to the 10 cm3 pipetted and the acid volume would be too high; the pipette and burette, on the other hand, are rinsed with the solutions they hold so that residual water does not dilute them.

items: Titration: unknown solution against a standard solution to the end point shown by an indicator (phenolphthalein pink to colourless as pH falls; fades as CO2 dissolves).

Procedure: pipette (water then NaOH) 10 cm3 NaOH + 1 to 2 drops indicator in a flask rinsed with water only; burette (water then HCl), funnel removed, bubble run out, initial reading with anti-parallax card; white paper; swirl; rough then three concordant readings within 0.1 cm3.
NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O; M1 V1 / n1 = M2 V2 / n2 gives the molarity of the base.
